Reviewer #1:

The revised manuscript is improved and adequately addresses most of my concerns. However, the authors expressed some confusion over my questions regarding the apparent discrepancy in OFF gating current kinetics, which I will attempt to clarify.

"We are somewhat confused about the reviewer 1 comment 3. As stated in Results the 𝜏𝐺−𝑂𝑁(𝑉) curves were fitted to a two-state model (𝜏(𝑉)=1/(𝛼(𝑉)+𝛽(𝑉)) where the forward (𝛼) and backward (𝛽) rate constants represent the resting-active (R-A) transitions of the voltage sensors determining the equilibrium constant of the VSD activation (𝐽(𝑉)=𝛼(𝑉)𝛽(𝑉)). Our statement that the main effect of Ca2+ is to slow down the OFF kinetics is based on the determination of 𝛼(𝑉) and 𝛽(𝑉) using the values of 𝜏𝐼𝐺−𝑂𝑁(𝑉) and J(V). This calculation indicates that 𝛽(𝑉) increase 10.9-fold when the Ca2+ concentration is increased to 100 μM (see legend in Figure 1), in a reasonable agreement with the large allosteric factor E. It is unclear to us why the reviewer is referring to Figure 2—figure supplement 1, a figure that is not directly comparable to Figure 1C."

My questions about gating current kinetics (Comments #3 in previous review, #1 in original review) relate in large part to the data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. I asked whether the difference in gating current kinetics shown for 0 and 10 μm Ca in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 are consistent with a large Q-V shift (as observed in 10 Ca). In particular, I noted that there is a relatively small change from 0 to 10 Ca in the time constant of the fast component of OFF current at -90 mV, which doesn't seem compatible with a large Q-V shift. The fast OFF component at -90 mV should be a relatively direct measure of the backward rate β (i.e. τ~=1/β). If there is a small change in ON kinetics and large Q-V shift, then there should be a large change in β and hence OFF kinetics. The authors make essentially the same prediction based on their fits to the ON kinetics in Figure 1C. But they do not include OFF data to directly confirm the prediction or address my concern.

"We would like to include the OFF time constant plot requested by the reviewer, but these kind of experiments are in extremely difficult to do at high Ca2+,.…"

I do not think that measurements of OFF kinetics at multiple voltages are necessary. Measurements at a single voltage like -90 mV should suffice. If OFF kinetics have not or cannot be measured at 100 Ca, then I suggest adding the ON kinetics at 10 Ca to Figure 1C together with OFF data at -90 mV for 0 and 10 Ca. Based on Figure 2—figure supplement 1, such data already exists.

results.result: Ca²⁺ binding to BK channels strongly facilitates voltage sensor domain (VSD) activation through direct energetic coupling. Saturating Ca²⁺ (100 μM) causes a large leftward shift in VSD activation (ΔVH = -142.6 ± 4.5 mV), decreasing the free energy by ~8 kJ/mol (ΔΔGVCa = -7.98 ± 0.27 kJ/mol) and amplifying the VSD equilibrium constant by a factor E = 26.4.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24, C29, C31-C32, and C67 collectively demonstrate strong Ca²⁺-VSD coupling through direct experimental measurements of gating charge movement at 0 and 100 μM Ca²⁺. The voltage shifts, free energy changes, and allosteric factors are quantified with error estimates and supported by data in Figures 1 and 2. The measurements are internally consistent and the methodology (gating current analysis) is appropriate for assessing VSD activation.

results.result: Fast ON-gating current relaxation reflects VSD movement in closed channel conformations, completing before channel opening at both 0 and 100 μM Ca²⁺. Ca²⁺ binding primarily affects the backward rate constant (β₀) of VSD activation, decreasing it from 76 ms⁻¹ at 0 Ca²⁺ to 7 ms⁻¹ at 100 μM Ca²⁺.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 and C30 are supported by kinetic analysis of gating and ionic currents shown in Figure 1A-B. The temporal separation between gating current decay and channel opening validates that QC measurements reflect closed-state VSD transitions. The rate constant changes are derived from fitting to a two-state model and are consistent with the observed voltage shifts.

results.result: Increasing internal Ca²⁺ concentration produces dose-dependent leftward shifts in QC(V) curves, with OFF-gating currents showing decreased amplitude and slower kinetics. At intermediate Ca²⁺ concentrations, OFF-gating currents exhibit fast and slow components, with the slow component increasing with Ca²⁺, reflecting increased channel open probability.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 describe Ca²⁺ dose-response effects on gating currents supported by data in Figure 2 and supplements. The dose-dependent shifts are quantified, and the biphasic OFF-gating current kinetics are analyzed. The interpretation that slow components reflect channel opening is consistent with established BK channel gating mechanisms and supported by the data showing charge recovery at hyperpolarized voltages.

results.result: Ca²⁺ binding to a single α-subunit affects all four VSDs equally (Scheme II), rather than only the VSD in the same subunit (Scheme I). Model II fits experimental QC(V,Ca²⁺) data significantly better than Model I based on Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), with Model I having negligible probability (wi = 10⁻⁴⁷). The constant slope (zQ) of QC(V) curves across Ca²⁺ concentrations supports the concerted interaction mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C53 and C96 present a rigorous model comparison using statistical criteria (AIC). The experimental observation of constant zQ across Ca²⁺ concentrations (C46, C51-C52) strongly discriminates between models. The analysis accounts for Ca²⁺ binding kinetics (C47-C48) and demonstrates that Scheme I cannot reproduce experimental data without violating biophysical constraints. The statistical evidence (C49-C50) overwhelmingly favors Scheme II.

results.result: Both RCK1 and RCK2 Ca²⁺-binding sites contribute approximately equally to VSD activation. Mutations disrupting RCK1 (D362A/D367A, M513I) or RCK2 (5D5A) each reduce the Ca²⁺-induced VSD shift by ~50% (ΔVH ≈ -65 to -75 mV vs. -143 mV for WT), with each site contributing ~4 kJ/mol to the free energy change. The additive effects suggest independent allosteric pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C66, C86-C87 demonstrate equal contributions from RCK1 and RCK2 sites through systematic mutagenesis experiments (Figures 5-6). Multiple independent mutations of each site produce similar ~50% reductions in VSD effects, with quantified free energy changes. The additivity of effects from the two sites is clearly demonstrated and supports independent pathways. The use of multiple mutations for RCK1 (D362A/D367A and M513I) strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: The measured Ca²⁺-induced VSD shift (ΔVH = -142.6 mV, ΔΔGVCa = -7.98 kJ/mol) agrees with previous work from the same laboratory but contradicts the smaller shift reported by Horrigan and Aldrich 2002 (ΔVH = -33 mV, ΔΔGVCa = -1.9 kJ/mol). The discrepancy is unlikely due to species differences given 96% identity between mouse and human BK channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 acknowledge a major discrepancy with foundational prior work (Horrigan and Aldrich 2002) that is not resolved. While the authors suggest experimental differences (expression system, Ca²⁺ concentration), they cannot definitively explain the 4-fold difference in energetic coupling. The high sequence identity argument (C70) is reasonable but does not exclude functional differences. This unresolved discrepancy creates uncertainty about the generalizability of the findings.

results.result: Fluorescence studies support bidirectional CTD-VSD coupling: Ca²⁺ binding causes VSD conformational changes (detected by voltage-clamp fluorometry), and VSD activation produces voltage-dependent gating ring rearrangements. VSD mutations alter gating ring motions while pore mutations do not, indicating VSD-mediated coupling.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 cite published fluorescence studies (Savalli et al. 2012, Miranda et al. 2013, 2018) that provide orthogonal evidence for CTD-VSD coupling. The cited work demonstrates bidirectional communication and identifies the VSD as the mediator of voltage-dependent gating ring motions. These prior results are consistent with and support the current gating current findings.

results.result: The structural basis for CTD-VSD coupling involves non-covalent interactions between the RCK1 N-lobe and VSD transmembrane segments (S0-S4), with domain swapping placing each RCK1 domain adjacent to the VSD of a neighboring subunit. Ca²⁺ binding triggers symmetric gating ring expansion that affects all VSDs through protein-protein interfaces, with the RCK1 site playing a primary role in VSD communication.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C84 synthesize structural and functional data from multiple cited studies to propose a mechanistic model. However, C77 is explicitly speculative, and the prior literature (C82-C84) suggested RCK1 dominance in VSD coupling, which contradicts the current finding of equal RCK1/RCK2 contributions. The structural model is plausible but not directly tested in this study, and the mechanistic details remain hypothetical.

results.result: The two RCK Ca²⁺-binding sites likely contribute independently to VSD modulation, though modest cooperativity between them cannot be excluded. Prior studies suggest intrasubunit cooperativity is more important than intersubunit cooperativity, with R514-Y904/E902 interactions as potential structural determinants.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C95 discuss cooperativity between Ca²⁺ sites but reach uncertain conclusions. The additive effects (C89) suggest independence, but cited literature (C90-C95) indicates modest cooperativity exists. The authors acknowledge they cannot definitively resolve this issue, and their modeling with cooperativity parameters produced unrealistic KD values. The structural basis for cooperativity (C91-C94) is speculative.

results.result: BK channels are homotetrameric voltage- and Ca²⁺-activated K⁺ channels with modular architecture including voltage-sensing domains (VSDs), Ca²⁺-sensing C-terminal domains (CTDs) containing RCK1 and RCK2 domains, and a pore domain. The RCK domains contain distinct high-affinity Ca²⁺-binding sites with different functional properties, and structural studies reveal CTD-VSD interfaces that mediate allosteric coupling.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C21, C54, C56, C59-C60, and C85 provide established background on BK channel structure and function, all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims accurately represent the current understanding of BK channel architecture, Ca²⁺ and voltage sensing mechanisms, and known structural features. The citations are appropriate and the claims are consistent with the field's knowledge.

results.result: The study used human BK α-subunit and site-specific mutants expressed in Xenopus oocytes. Gating currents were recorded using inside-out patch clamp with 1 ms voltage steps, 20 kHz filtering, 500 kHz sampling, and P/4 leak subtraction. QC was determined by integrating the first 50-100 μs of ON-gating currents fitted to single exponentials.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C107 describe standard electrophysiological methods that are appropriate for measuring gating currents. The technical details (filtering, sampling rates, leak subtraction protocol) are adequate for the fast gating current measurements. The Ca²⁺ concentration determination using software and electrode validation (C105) is appropriate. The data analysis approach (C107) is standard and properly cited.

results.result: Ca2+ binding to the RCK domains produces a large leftward shift (~143 mV) in the voltage-sensor activation curve (QC(V)), corresponding to a ~8 kJ/mol decrease in free energy and a 26-fold increase in the voltage sensor equilibrium constant. This demonstrates strong energetic coupling between Ca2+ sensors and voltage-sensing domains.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge this as an important finding, they express significant concerns about the magnitude of the shift compared to Horrigan and Aldrich (2002), who reported only -33 mV. Reviewer #1 states the claim that 'this result resolves a previous debate' does not appear reasonable since 'for the authors merely to replicate their previous findings does not seem sufficient in the absence of a clear source of error.' Reviewers request more detailed kinetic analysis and clarification of methodological differences to reconcile the discrepancy.

results.result: The fast ON-gating current relaxation completes before channel opening at both 0 and 100 μM Ca2+, indicating that the measured gating charge (QC) reflects voltage sensor movement in the closed state, independent of Ca2+ concentration.
results.evaluation: Reviewer #2 requests additional support for this claim, stating 'This statement could be supported by showing ionic currents along with gating currents at the same voltages. The comparison in high [Ca] (≥10 µM) would be particularly helpful.' Reviewers want to ensure QC is adequately distinguished from QSS and not contaminated by channel opening, particularly at high Ca2+.

results.result: Increasing internal Ca2+ produces a dose-dependent leftward shift of QC(V) curves with modifications to OFF-gating current kinetics, including slower decay and increased contribution of a slow component reflecting increased channel open probability.
results.evaluation: Reviewer #1 notes concerns about kinetic analysis, stating 'it would be helpful to compare τfast(V) relations in the presence and absence of Ca' and questions how 'small changes in kinetics including little effect of Ca on ON kinetics and a 2.5-fold slowing of the fast component of OFF kinetics' can be reconciled with 'the propose 26-fold change in equilibrium constant.' The reviewers request more complete kinetic characterization to support the equilibrium shift claims.

results.result: Model comparison using Akaike Information Criterion shows that Scheme II (concerted mechanism where Ca2+ binding to one subunit affects all four VSDs equally) fits the experimental data significantly better than Scheme I (independent mechanism where Ca2+ binding affects only the VSD in the same subunit).
results.evaluation: Reviewer #1 raises substantial concerns about the model testing: 'Both models incorporate a single Ca site per subunit, inconsistent with the conclusion from Figure 4 that both sites contribute equally to voltage sensor activation. An extended version of scheme I with 2 binding sites would predict QC(V) curves that are essentially a sum of 3 Boltzmann functions and should therefore better fit the data.' Reviewer #3 notes 'although the authors suggest that HA Model II in Figure 2 fits their data better than HA Model I, it seems that neither model fits the data well.' The reviewers request testing with two Ca2+ binding sites per subunit.

results.result: Mutations disrupting either the RCK1 Ca2+-binding site (D362A/D367A, M513I) or the RCK2 Ca2+ bowl (5D5A) each reduce the Ca2+-induced QC(V) shift by approximately 50%, indicating that both high-affinity Ca2+-binding sites contribute equally (~4 kJ/mol each) and independently to VSD activation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these mutational findings without significant critique. Reviewer #3 states the authors 'present compelling evidence that Ca-binding to the cytosolic domain does allosterically influence VSD equilibrium and, furthermore, that each of the two Ca binding sites on a single BK α subunit independently, and largely additively, influence the VSD equilibrium.' The equal contribution of both sites is well-supported by the experimental data.

results.result: Ca2+ binding primarily affects the backward rate constant (β0) of the voltage sensor resting-active transition, decreasing it from 76 ms⁻¹ at 0 Ca2+ to 7-10.6 ms⁻¹ at elevated Ca2+.
results.evaluation: Reviewer #1 questions the kinetic analysis, noting 'Surprisingly, the present study also describes small changes in kinetics including little effect of Ca on ON kinetics and a 2.5-fold slowing of the fast component of OFF kinetics in 10 μm Ca at -90 mV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). How can these effects be reconciled with the propose 26-fold change in equilibrium constant?' The reviewers request more complete OFF kinetics data to confirm the predictions.

results.result: The observed large Ca2+-induced shift in QC(V) agrees with previous reports from the same laboratory but contradicts the smaller shift reported by Horrigan and Aldrich (2002), a discrepancy unlikely due to species differences given 96% identity between mouse and human BK channels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly critique the handling of this discrepancy. The editorial summary states 'it is not sufficient to simply claim the issue is resolved since the present results confirm earlier results from this same lab. That is ignoring the issue.' Reviewers request 'a rigorous, scholarly assessment of potential reasons for differences' and 'an objective comparison of the similarities and differences in what each group was measuring and how the gating current was determined.'

results.result: Previous fluorescence and functional studies demonstrate voltage-dependent Ca2+ binding to RCK1, Ca2+-induced perturbations of VSD movements, and that RCK1 site occupancy is primarily responsible for CTD-VSD allosteric coupling and voltage-dependent gating ring rearrangements.
results.evaluation: These claims are based on well-cited previous work and are not challenged by reviewers. They provide important context for interpreting the current findings. Reviewers accept these as established background without raising concerns.

results.result: Structural studies reveal that the RCK1 N-lobe contacts the VSD and S4-S5 linker through non-covalent interactions, with this interface rearranging upon Ca2+ binding, suggesting Ca2+-induced conformational changes are transmitted to the pore domain via the VSD.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these structural interpretations from published cryo-EM studies. Reviewer #2 notes 'based on previously published cryo-EM structures the authors favor the mechanism of the non-covalent VSD-CTD interactions' but points out 'the present data seems not sufficient to exclude the contribution by the other mechanism' (C-linker pulling). The structural basis is accepted but mechanistic details remain open.

results.result: BK channels are tetrameric voltage- and Ca2+-gated K+ channels with each subunit containing a voltage-sensing domain and a C-terminal domain with two distinct RCK Ca2+-binding sites (RCK1 and RCK2) that differ in affinity, selectivity, voltage dependence, and contribution to gating.
results.evaluation: These are well-established background claims supported by extensive citations to published literature. Reviewers do not challenge these foundational descriptions of BK channel structure and function.

results.result: At very negative voltages (-150 mV and -200 mV) with 100 μM internal Ca2+, the charge displaced during ON gating current is fully recovered during OFF gating current.
results.evaluation: This observation is presented as experimental data without reviewer challenge. It supports the reversibility of voltage sensor movement under these conditions.

results.result: The RCK1 and RCK2 high-affinity Ca2+-binding sites are responsible for physiological Ca2+ sensitivity, with specific residues (D362/D367 in RCK1, D894-D898 in Ca2+ bowl) critical for Ca2+ coordination and M513 important for RCK1 site conformation.
results.evaluation: These claims are based on well-established mutagenesis studies cited in the literature. Reviewers do not challenge these structural and functional assignments of specific residues.

results.result: The two RCK Ca2+-binding sites likely contribute independently to VSD modulation, though modest intrasubunit cooperativity between RCK1 and RCK2 sites may exist through structural connections like R514-Y904/E902 interactions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this interpretation as consistent with both the current data and previous literature. The discussion of potential cooperativity is appropriately cautious and supported by citations.

results.result: Scanning mutagenesis indicates that residues in the βA-αC region of RCK1 N-terminal subdomain are involved in allosteric connection of Ca2+-dependent activation mediated by RCK1 site occupancy.
results.evaluation: This claim is based on cited mutagenesis studies and is not challenged by reviewers. It provides supporting evidence for the RCK1-VSD coupling mechanism.

results.result: The physical CTD-VSD interface provides the structure capable of mediating crosstalk between Ca2+ and voltage sensory modules and their synergy in activating the pore domain.
results.evaluation: This general mechanistic framework is supported by multiple cited structural and functional studies. Reviewers do not challenge this conceptual model, though they note that specific mechanistic details remain to be fully resolved.

results.result: The study used human BK α-subunit and specific Ca2+-binding site mutants expressed in Xenopus oocytes, with gating currents measured using cut-open oocyte voltage clamp with specific filtering, sampling, and analysis protocols.
results.evaluation: While reviewers do not directly challenge the methods as described, they request substantial additional methodological details and clarification. Reviewer #1 asks for 'examples of fits used to determine QC' and clarification of the grounding scheme. Reviewers also note concerns about potential differences in methodology that might explain discrepancies with Horrigan and Aldrich (2002). The editorial summary emphasizes the need for 'an objective comparison of the similarities and differences in what each group was measuring and how the gating current was determined.'

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the same claims (C22-C24, C29, C31-C32, C67) about Ca²⁺-VSD coupling and voltage shifts. OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED with strong experimental measurements, while peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN due to concerns about the magnitude discrepancy with Horrigan and Aldrich (2002) and insufficient explanation of methodological differences.

Both address kinetic analysis claims (C25-C28). OpenEval finds the temporal separation between gating current and channel opening SUPPORTED, while peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN and request additional ionic current comparisons at the same voltages, particularly at high Ca²⁺, to ensure QC is not contaminated by channel opening.

Both evaluate Ca²⁺ dose-response effects on gating currents (C33-C38). OpenEval finds the data SUPPORTED, while peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, questioning how small kinetic changes can be reconciled with the proposed 26-fold equilibrium constant change and requesting more complete kinetic characterization.

Both assess model comparison claims (C40-C53, C96). OpenEval finds the statistical evidence SUPPORTED and favoring Scheme II, while peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, noting that both models use only one Ca²⁺ site per subunit (inconsistent with Figure 4 findings) and that neither model fits the data well. Reviewers request testing with two Ca²⁺ binding sites per subunit.

Both evaluate claims about equal contributions from RCK1 and RCK2 sites (C55-C66, C86-C87). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers find this SUPPORTED, with peer reviewers describing the evidence as 'compelling' that both sites independently and additively influence VSD equilibrium.

Both address the discrepancy with Horrigan and Aldrich (2002) (C68-C70). Both rate this UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes the discrepancy is not resolved and creates uncertainty about generalizability. Peer reviewers strongly critique the handling, stating it's insufficient to claim the issue is resolved by replicating earlier results from the same lab, and request rigorous assessment of potential reasons for differences.

Both discuss fluorescence studies and CTD-VSD coupling (C71-C75 overlap). OpenEval finds the cited prior work SUPPORTED as providing orthogonal evidence. Peer reviewers also find these background claims SUPPORTED without challenge, accepting them as established context for interpreting current findings.

Partial overlap on structural interpretations (C76, C78-C80). OpenEval rates mechanistic model claims UNCERTAIN due to speculation and contradictions with prior literature. Peer reviewers find structural basis SUPPORTED from cryo-EM studies but note that mechanistic details (e.g., C-linker pulling vs. non-covalent interactions) remain open and current data insufficient to exclude alternative mechanisms.

Both evaluate cooperativity between Ca²⁺ sites (C88-C95). OpenEval rates this UNCERTAIN due to conflicting evidence and inability to resolve the issue definitively. Peer reviewers rate it SUPPORTED, accepting the interpretation as consistent with data and appropriately cautious in discussing potential cooperativity.

Both address established background on BK channel structure and function (C1-C9, C13-C17 overlap). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers find these claims SUPPORTED as well-established foundational knowledge with appropriate citations to published literature.

Both evaluate methods claims (C97-C107). OpenEval finds the methods SUPPORTED as appropriate and standard. Peer reviewers rate them UNCERTAIN, not directly challenging the methods but requesting substantial additional methodological details, clarification of grounding scheme, and objective comparison with Horrigan and Aldrich (2002) methodology to explain discrepancies.

Minor overlap on kinetic claims (C30). OpenEval finds kinetic analysis SUPPORTED in R2. Peer R6 questions reconciliation of small kinetic changes with large equilibrium constant changes, rating UNCERTAIN and requesting more complete OFF kinetics data.

Minor overlap on charge recovery observation (C39). OpenEval includes this in SUPPORTED dose-response analysis (R3). Peer reviewers accept this as experimental data without challenge (R11, SUPPORTED), supporting reversibility of voltage sensor movement.
Overlap on mutagenesis background (C54, C56, C59-C60, C85). Both find these SUPPORTED as well-established structural and functional assignments from cited literature without challenge.

Overlap on prior literature suggesting RCK1 dominance (C82-C84). OpenEval notes this contradicts current findings of equal contributions, rating mechanistic model UNCERTAIN. Peer reviewers accept these as established background (SUPPORTED) providing context.

Minor overlap on mutagenesis evidence (C81). OpenEval includes this in UNCERTAIN mechanistic synthesis (R8). Peer reviewers accept this specific claim as SUPPORTED based on cited studies, providing evidence for RCK1-VSD coupling.

Minor overlap on general mechanistic framework (C12). OpenEval includes this in SUPPORTED background claims (R10). Peer reviewers also find this conceptual model SUPPORTED by multiple studies, though specific mechanistic details remain unresolved.
